items.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
items.description:
arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the
items.summary: A new method called "Refusal Aversion in the Wild" aims to measure the impact of LLM refusals on users, addressing a previously overlooked area in deployed large language models. This measurement could provide crucial insights into user engagement and satisfaction, helping improve model performance and usability.
items.summary_detailed: The paper "Refusal Aversion in the Wild" introduces a new causal measurement method to quantify the impact of refusals from Large Language Models (LLMs) on user engagement. Researchers are focusing on how users react when LLMs decline requests, which has not been systematically measured before due to the sheer volume of interactions and the complexity of attributing disengagement solely to model refusals. This method could provide insights into improving user experience and model utility in real-world applications.
items.summary_bullets:
• Deployed LLMs receive hundreds of millions of conversations daily.
• A significant portion of user requests are refused by these models.
• The user impact of refusals has not been measured in production models.

items.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
items.description:
arXiv:2611.21648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night
items.summary: Researchers tested the "overfitted brain" hypothesis by having an LLM named Claude Opus 5.5 rewrite its text memory nightly, finding if this mimics dream-like replay to prevent overfitting—testing whether such processes could enable dreams in artificial agents.
items.summary_detailed: Researchers tested the "overfitted brain hypothesis" proposed by Hoel (2021), which suggests dreams help prevent overfitting to recent experiences, on an LLM agent named Claude Opus 5.5 that retains learned information in a text memory and rewrites it nightly. The broader impact could provide insights into how artificial intelligence systems might be designed to better handle and generalize from large amounts of data.
items.summary_bullets:
• Hoel's overfitted brain hypothesis suggests dreams distort replayed experiences.
• The study tests this theory using an LLM named Claude Opus 5.5.
• Claude stores learned information in text memory which it rewrites nightly.
